Multimodal Filesystem Memory

Multimodal Filesystem Memory Agent Reaches 10/10 on Long-Horizon Mine Diamond from Scratch Task

Mining a diamond from an empty inventory takes 10 gated milestones and almost all of a 12,000-step budget; killing the ender dragon takes 24. Every step returns another 640×360 image, and a fact learned at step 2,000 still has to be usable at step 11,000 — more than any context window holds. MFM puts the whole record on a filesystem — text as the index, images as the evidence — and a periodic induction turn compiles it into a structured world model. Hand that compiled memory to the next life, and nothing else, and the third generation became the first run of either protocol to reach the diamond: 10/10 at step 11,444.

multimodal memory MCU benchmark 2 long-horizon tasks 10 & 24 milestones 12,000 steps

01 — Motivation

Why these tasks need a filesystem

Both tasks start from an empty inventory in a freshly generated world, and both are scored by how many ordered milestones the agent reaches: 10 for the diamond, 24 for the ender dragon. The ordering is real tool-tier gating rather than bookkeeping — cobblestone needs a wooden pickaxe, iron ore a stone pickaxe, diamond an iron pickaxe.

Written out as a milestone list, either task looks like a recipe. What makes it hard is that the recipe has to be carried out by an agent with a body, standing inside a world it can see only a cone of. Every standard difficulty of embodied intelligence shows up here in a concrete form, and the diamond run is the clearest place to see each one:

  • Partial observability. The observation is one 640×360 first-person frame per step, and for most of the episode that frame is a few blocks of dim tunnel wall in which the difference between stone and iron ore is a few pixels of contrast. Whatever is behind the agent, around the corner, or under the floor is not in the observation at all. In the winning run the diamond item, once mined, was a few blocks west and out of frame; the recovery sweep walked east, and the only way to know it had walked the wrong way was the record of the drop’s coordinates.
  • Long-horizon planning. Many milestones, each gated on the previous milest, and tasks need almost full of the 12,000 max steps to fully solve. The plan has to hold across the whole chain: a single missed craft near the top caps everything below it, and a plan executed flawlessly against a stale goal — still chasing iron when the budget can afford exactly one more milestone — scores the same as no plan.
  • Spatial reasoning. The agent constantly sees things it cannot use yet — an ore vein it lacks the pickaxe for, a cave mouth, a shaft that will be the fastest way down for the rest of the episode. Getting back to any of them thousands of steps later is a memory problem before it is a navigation one: the record has to say where the thing was and what it looked like, and be searchable by place rather than scanned from the beginning.
  • Dynamics and world modeling. An embodied plan is a count of ticks: how long a block takes to break, how far a tunnel advances per cycle, what opens under the agent when it digs straight down. Those constants are properties of the physics, not the task, and a plan built on a guess at them issues the wrong number of actions and comes back with nothing.
  • Exploration. Ore is found by covering ground, and the agent cannot see what it has not covered. “Explored a lot” and “covered x in [−200, 50]” are different facts, and the difference is whether the next 2,000 steps repeat the last 2,000. Cheap detectors help and mislead in equal measure: across one campaign the ore sentinel fired 4 times, on grass, water over stone, gravel and bark, and every flag had to be settled by going back to the frame it fired on.

The best run on this page reached the diamond at step 11,444 of 12,000, which means a constant measured at step 800 and a shaft dug at step 3,000 both have to still be usable at step 11,000 — and every one of those steps returned another 640×360 image. The episode generates far more experience than a context window can hold, and the parts most worth having are the oldest — where the ore was, which shaft already dead-ended, how far a tunnel actually advances per swing. Before any of the difficulties above can be reasoned about, the facts they turn on have to be remembered.

So the memory has to live somewhere other than the prompt, and the answer is a filesystem. The following 3 naive approaches each get partway there, and each breaks in its own way.

Keep beliefs in the prompt and they cannot outgrow the context window. A typed belief graph is the right structure, but re-sending every belief every step forces a cap on how many the agent can hold — a limit set by the context.

Keep an unbounded log on disk and the record survives, but with no structure over it beyond grep: the agent re-derives its understanding from raw lines on every turn, at a cost that grows with the episode.

Keep observations in the prompt and almost none survive. Images are the most expensive thing a context can hold, so only the last few frames stay and everything older is gone — including the one frame that would settle the question the agent is stuck on.

MFM answers all three at once. The belief graph lives on the filesystem, so it outlives the context; frames are written there too, addressed by path from the text record, so the visual past is retrievable rather than expiring; and a periodic pass compiles the raw record into a world model with entities, topology, and causal structure.

ApproachWhere knowledge livesBinding limitWhat MFM does instead
Beliefs in the promptA prompt section, re-sent every step8 nodes rendered; the graph can never exceed the contextThe graph lives in hypotheses/graph.json. The cap now bounds what is rendered, not what is known
An unbounded logAn append-only file, greppedNo structure; understanding re-derived from raw lines each turnA periodic induction pass compiles the log into five documents
Observations in the promptThe last k frames, re-sentImages are the priciest tokens there are, so k stays tiny and everything older expiresFrames live in episodes/*/frames/, addressed by path from the log. The agent opens — and pays for — only the ones it wants

02 — Tasks

What the agent is actually doing

The two tasks on this page — mine_diamond_from_scratch and kill_ender_dragon — come from the Minecraft benchmark built for Berkeley RDI’s AgentX / AgentBeats, whose Minecraft green agent scenario defines the milestone lists and step budgets we run against unmodified.

Neither task is scored pass/fail. Each config lists an ordered progression of milestones — 10 for the diamond task, 24 for the dragon — and the score is how many were reached, in any order, before the step budget runs out. What the agent is handed at step 0 is one line of text.

The two are not independent benchmarks. The diamond task is a prefix of the dragon task: its 10 milestones appear, in the same order, as the dragon's first 10.

The dependencies are real tool-tier gates, not bookkeeping. Cobblestone cannot be mined without a wooden pickaxe; iron ore needs a stone pickaxe; the ingot needs a furnace and fuel; diamond needs an iron pickaxe; obsidian needs a diamond one. A single missed craft near the top of the chain caps everything below it, which is why the crafting GUI — and not exploration — is where these runs are won or lost.

What a run looks like from inside

These are unmodified frames from one episode of the full method on mine_diamond_from_scratch, each captured at the exact step its milestone fired. They are the same 640×360 images the model is handed as its observation.

Two things worth noticing. The GUI frames are the whole difficulty of the benchmark in one picture — there is no craft action, so a recipe is a cursor landing on a slot. And the underground frames are what the agent has to plan from for most of the episode: a dim tunnel where the difference between stone and iron ore is a few pixels of contrast in a wall.

03 — Memory

Memory is a multimodal filesystem, and two kinds of turn drive it

The agent's memory is a directory that persists for the whole episode, and it holds two kinds of thing: text the agent can grep, and pictures it can open. It is read programmatically — it is far too large to read by eye, and reading it by eye is exactly the error the design exists to avoid.

The load-bearing detail is not the layout but who is allowed to write what. A belief the agent holds and a fact the environment reported must never land in the same file. If they do, the discipline layer has nothing to check a claim against — and an agent that can rewrite events.jsonl can make any goal true by editing a file. The harness fails loudly on any modification to a file it owns.

PathWriterContents
logs.txtHarnessAppend-only trace: every action, the state that followed, the agent's own prior analyses. Grepped, never read whole
events/events.jsonlHarnessOne line per statistic that moves — mine_block, craft_item, pickup, kill_entity. A craft that does not appear here did not happen
maps/visited.csvHarnessEvery position occupied, with its step number
episodes/*/frames/HarnessThe first-person view per step, referenced from the log by path so the agent opens only what it wants
world_model/AgentFive structured documents, rewritten by induction and read by every act turn
hypotheses/graph.jsonAgentThe belief DAG, mirrored to disk every step
procedures/AgentOne file per action sequence that worked, in enough detail to replay it
entities/ · locations/AgentOne file per kind of thing observed, one per named place

A claim and its check must not share a source

A belief store the world cannot correct is a way to make a mistake permanent. In an earlier campaign a run confirmed “there is a spruce door on the front wall” at step 2, from 8 blocks away, and the belief rode the prompt at confidence 0.95 for the remaining 198 steps while the agent tried to open a door it had never seen. 70 of 177 goal nodes finished above 0.9 and unverified.

The check is continuous because there is no moment to gate: an episode ends only when the step budget runs out. Every step, each goal hypothesis is compared against the ledger, and a goal the model marks confirmed that the ledger has not verified is reverted on the spot — confidence drops to 0.6 and the statement itself is prefixed [unverified: the environment has not confirmed this], because the statement is what the prompt renders back and marking only the status would leave the model reading its own claim as fact. This fires at step 40 instead of step 300, and it fires every time. The remaining mechanics — closed-loop procedures that report what changed rather than what they attempted, a GUI cursor measured from the frame instead of dead-reckoned, per-arm isolation of ports, sessions and configuration — are in the repository README.

Text as an index into pictures

The filesystem is multimodal in a specific and cheap way. The observation stream is written to disk as PNGs, and the text record carries pointers into it. When a detector fires, the harness saves the frame it fired on and writes that path into logs.txt as a [FRAME] line naming that file and not a later one — because by the time the agent reads the note, the thing it needs to look at has usually scrolled out of view. The act turn can then open it: ./tools/zoom.py <frame> <x> <y> <w> <h> crops and magnifies any region, which is what it takes when the answer is a few pixels of contrast in a wall.

This buys retrieval over images without paying to carry them. A 12,000-step episode produces 12,000 frames; a run’s curated set keeps 56 to 133 of them, because those are the ones a text line ever pointed at. Everything else is on disk and free. The model pays for a frame only when it decides it needs to look — and because the pointer is a path in a file rather than an attachment in a context, a frame from step 1,518 is exactly as reachable at step 9,000 as it was when it was written.

It does decide, and the deciding is load-bearing. Across one campaign the ore sentinel fired 4 times; all 4 were false positives — grass top, water over stone, a dirt-and-gravel wall, tree bark — and in every case the model opened the named frame, zoomed it, and rejected the flag. 4 of 4. A cheap detector that a careful reader can overrule is a different component from a detector that has to be right on its own, and the difference is entirely the ability to go back and look.

Memory with a position in it

What separates this from a chat agent’s memory is that the agent has a body. Almost everything worth keeping is indexed by where rather than by when, and three consequences of that run through the whole schema.

The observation is egocentric and partial. The agent sees a cone of a world it is standing inside, so the only way to know what it has not seen is to have recorded where it went. maps/visited.csv logs every position occupied with the step number, which turns “have I already searched here?” into a query rather than a recollection — and spatial.md is written against it, which is why covered x in [-200, 50] is worth more than explored a lot. The difference between those two sentences is whether the next 2,000 steps repeat the last 2,000.

The facts it needs are metric. An embodied plan is computed, not described: blocks moved per travel entry, attack ticks per log, degrees per camera delta. dynamics.md exists to hold numbers, because a plan built on “mining takes a while” issues the wrong count of ticks and comes back with nothing. Getting these constants wrong is the most common reason a plan does nothing at all.

Coordinates outlive goals. The world is generated deterministically from a seed, so an ore site at a fixed position, a shaft route, a hazard at known coordinates stay true for the rest of the episode — and, it turns out, across episodes. That is what makes the relay results possible: what one run learns about a place is still true for the next run, and still true even when the next run was asked to do something else entirely.

The five documents

Structure is imposed rather than left to the model, because ad-hoc layouts diverge across episodes and induction then cannot merge two episodes' knowledge. Each document is truncated per document when the act turn reads it, so a large causal.md cannot push spatial.md out of the prompt entirely.

  • spatial.md — coordinates, topology, routes, and regions already covered, every claim cited against visited.csv.
  • semantic.md — what kinds of thing exist and what they afford: what an entity drops, what breaks it, what tool tier it needs.
  • dynamics.md — action → consequence with numbers: the measured constants the act turn plans against.
  • procedural.md — ordered recipes that worked, with preconditions and the events.jsonl line proving they worked. Recipes that failed belong here too, marked failed.
  • causal.md — dependencies: what must be true before what, with the milestone list as its spine.

Two kinds of turn over one filesystem

Most agent loops have one kind of turn. This one has two, and the split is what makes a 12,000-step episode affordable at all.

Act turnInduction turn
FiresWhen the action queue runs dryEvery 600 steps, or early on a stall
ReadsThe newest frame, the milestone checklist, the compiled documents, a view of the belief graphThe accumulated filesystem: logs, events, positions, frames, the whole graph
Writesactions.json — up to 40 plan entries that refill the queueThe five documents, plus hypotheses_ops.json. No actions at all

A single-turn design has to re-derive its understanding from raw log lines on every call. Either the log stays small and the agent forgets, or the turns get slow and a long episode becomes unaffordable. Compiling periodically means the frequent turn reads a summary and the expensive turn amortizes over hundreds of steps.

Induction is also the only turn that looks back — the only place a belief formed 400 steps ago and never revisited can be settled — and the only turn that questions the objective. It closes causal.md with a goal check: what each unmet milestone still needs, what those steps cost by the agent's own measured constants, and the cheapest unmet milestone to bank first if the budget is tighter than the plan. Flawless execution of a stale goal scores zero.

Stall-triggered induction

When 12 consecutive act turns pass with no verified movement in ground truth — no milestone, no inventory change — induction fires early on a diagnosis prompt instead of a housekeeping one. It must name the failing procedure, cite the step numbers behind it, and state the one observation that would separate its explanation from the next best one. That observation is what the next act turns go and get.

04 — Results

Results

The three arms, and what separates them

memory is the only thing the arms are allowed to differ in. All three run the identical execution engine, perception stack, procedure library, caps, and task knowledge — and the prompt text describing surfaces they share is kept word-for-word identical. The baseline arm is the protocol from PRO-LONG — an append-only log the model greps, with nothing compiled on top of it.

ArmMemoryIsolates
worldmodelFive compiled documents, belief DAG, discipline layer, structured event and position channelsThe full method
wmliteThe logbook substrate plus one compiled document kept current by induction. No graph, no ops, no discipline, no taxonomyWhether compiling the past beats grepping it raw — that claim alone
logbookOne append-only log the model greps, plus whatever it chooses to save. Induction disabledThe unstructured-log baseline — PRO-LONG's protocol — on identical hardware and skills

Isolation is scripted, not described. Two runs that differ in a shared credential, a shared session store, or an inherited config file differ in ways no log line records — so each arm gets its own ports, output directory, and model home, and the launcher aborts rather than reclaiming a busy port. An ablation described in prose is not an ablation.

The three regimes, and what each asks

Every run on this page holds the same things fixed — byte-identical chassis, the same model at the same reasoning effort, world seed 0 and a fixed spawn, the same 12,000-step budget. The single variable is what the run starts by remembering. That variable takes three settings, and the three ask different questions.

RegimeWhat the run begins withThe question it answers
1 · From scratchAn empty memory directory. Everything the run knows at step 12,000 it learned in this episodeWhat is the memory protocol worth within a single life?
2 · Relay, same taskThe final memory of an earlier run on this same task, copied in before step 1 — diamond → diamond, dragon → dragonDoes experience accumulate across lives, or does each generation start over?
3 · Relay, across tasksThe final memory of an earlier run on the other task — diamond → dragon, dragon → diamondIs what got written down knowledge of the world, or only of the goal?

The relay is mechanical and narrow: --seed-memory <parent>/memory copies the parent's final memory directory into the child's workspace, and nothing else crosses. Fresh world, fresh inventory, fresh position, fresh session. The child is told in its standing preamble that the world has reset — coordinates and terrain stay valid, anything built or emptied is restored, stale goals must be re-derived.

1 — From scratch: what the protocol is worth in one life

The controlled ablation runs both memory protocols with no inheritance at all, and records the step each milestone landed on. The score is a count, so it is blind to what each milestone cost; reading the gaps rather than the totals is what separates the arms.

Within one life the advantage is task-dependent, and on the shorter task it reverses. On mine_diamond_from_scratch both arms finish at 8/10 — an identical score — but the logbook arm gets there faster on 6 of the 8, reaching iron ore 1,587 steps earlier and the ingot 2,632 earlier. The worldmodel arm leads only on the 2 early crafting milestones. On this task, compiling the past bought nothing that grepping it raw did not.

On kill_ender_dragon the picture inverts. The arms track together for 3 milestones, then separate at mine_cobblestone — a 1,976-step gap that never closes — and the worldmodel arm banks 5 further milestones the logbook arm never reaches, finishing 11/24 against 6/24 and picking up a diamond at step 11,977 along the way. The logbook failure is not the budget running out: that arm reached its last milestone at step 5,124 with 6,876 steps still unspent, and spent them without finding iron. That is a search failure, not an exhaustion failure.

A later wave re-ran the from-scratch condition on the worldmodel arm alone, on the same commit family as the relay runs below: dm15z_wm_high reached 7/10 on diamond and kd15z_wm_high 7/24 on the dragon. Those two are the controls the relay results are measured against, because they share a wave with them; the 8/10 and 11/24 above are the best from-scratch runs on record across all waves.

2 — Relay within the same task: diamond → diamond, dragon → dragon

On the diamond the generations compound, and the third one closes the task. Starting from the 7/10 from-scratch control, one relay generation reaches 9/10 (dm15_wm_high, seeded from dm14x), and the next reaches 10/10 — dm16_wm_high, seeded from dm15, the first run of either protocol to take the task all the way to the diamond. What each generation hands down is a registry of verified world facts — ore sites, shaft routes, hazards at fixed coordinates in a world that resets deterministically — plus procedures debugged in earlier lives. dm16's registry entry for the diamond site at y12 is the artefact that made its run fast.

On the dragon it does not compound. Both children of kd14x land on 9/24 — ahead of the 7/24 control, but 2 milestones behind the 11/24 parent whose memory they inherited. Same-task inheritance on this task moved the floor up and the ceiling down. The dragon's 24 milestones run far past the shared prefix into the End, and the parent memory carries little that is verified about that stretch.

Inheritance by itself is not the lever — distillation is. The symmetric control hands the child the parent's raw logs.txt instead of a distilled memory (--seed-log): everything the worldmodel arm's compilation was made from, none of the compiling. On the diamond that run scored 6/10, below the 7/10 from-scratch control — an inherited log made the agent worse than no inheritance at all. On the dragon it managed 8/24, one above the control and three below the distilled relay.

3 — Relay across tasks: diamond → dragon, dragon → diamond

The two tasks share their first 8 milestones, from mine_log through iron_pickaxe, in one deterministic world. If what the memory holds is knowledge of that world rather than of the goal, it should transfer across the task boundary. It does — on both tasks the cross-task child matched or beat what same-task inheritance managed, and on the dragon it beat it outright.

dm14x_wm_high started from kd12's dragon memory — a parent that had scored only 7/24 on its own task — and reached 9/10 on the diamond, 2 above the control and better than any diamond run before it. kd14x_wm_high started from dm11c's diamond memory and reached 11/24, 4 above the control, the best dragon run of the relay era and a tie with the from-scratch record set by kd6_wm_high. On the dragon, cross-task inheritance beat same-task inheritance: 11/24 against the 9/24 its own children managed.

How to read this

One run per cell, one seed, best-of rather than sampled means: these are existence proofs, not effect sizes. Three limits are worth stating plainly. The diamond reversal in regime 1 rests on a single pair. The relay comparisons are only clean within a wave — dm6/kd6 ran an earlier commit than the relay era, so the dashed baselines in the figure are the same-wave controls, not the all-time bests. And the best dragon run on record from scratch (11/24) equals the best relayed one, so on that task the relay has beaten its own control but not the ceiling. Six of the relay-era arms also flew through a 2h20m provider outage; the evaluator holds its request while the agent retries, so no step budget was lost, but their model-call counts are inflated and call efficiency cannot be attributed to memory maturity in this batch. Turn economics and the discipline counters are reported per run in each trajectory's worldmodel_report.json; the cross-arm actuation counters are near-identical by design, which is the check that the ablation held.

The run that closed the task

The run at the top of the page is the 10/10 from regime 2: dm16_wm_high, the third distilled-relay generation on mine_diamond_from_scratch — started from the final memory of dm15, which had itself been started from dm14x, which had been started from a dragon run's memory. Every generation in that chain shares the chassis, model, world seed, spawn and step budget used everywhere above; the only thing that changed down the line is what each run began by remembering. It reached all 10 milestones for a score of 100.0, the diamond landing at step 11,444 of 12,000: mine_log@480, crafting_table@1131, wooden_pickaxe@1323, mine_cobblestone@2085, stone_pickaxe@3427, furnace@3494, mine_iron_ore@4446, iron_ingot@5568, iron_pickaxe@6330, diamond@11444.

05 — Discussion

What the runs settle, and what they leave open

Compiled memory is not uniformly better — it pays where the horizon is long. On the 10-milestone diamond task from scratch, the logbook arm matched the worldmodel arm's score and reached 6 of the 8 shared milestones sooner. On the 24-milestone dragon the two arms separate at mine_cobblestone and never re-converge, 11/24 against 6/24, with the losing arm sitting on 6,876 unspent steps. The difference between the two tasks is not difficulty but failure mode: on the short one the bottleneck is executing a recipe the model already knows, and a raw log is enough to keep the recipe straight. On the long one the bottleneck is search — and a structured record of where you have already dug is worth more than a transcript you have to re-read to find out.

What transfers is distillation, not inheritance. The raw-log control is the sharpest number on the page: hand a child everything the compilation was made from, minus the compiling, and it scores 6/10 on the diamond — below the 7/10 of a child that inherited nothing. An undigested parent log is not neutral, it is a liability: it spends context and offers claims the child has no way to check. The distilled relay off comparable parents reached 9/10, then 10/10.

What gets distilled is knowledge of the world, not of the goal. A dragon parent that had managed only 7/24 on its own task produced the best diamond run to that point (9/10), and a diamond parent produced the best dragon run of the relay era (11/24) — beating the 9/24 that the dragon's own children managed. Ore sites, shaft routes, hazards at fixed coordinates and procedures debugged in an earlier life are properties of a deterministic world; they do not know which task asked for them. That is the result the grounding discipline is meant to buy: a registry entry only crosses the generation boundary if the environment confirmed it, so what the child inherits is checkable regardless of what the parent was trying to do.

The image channel is held constant, not ablated. Every arm on this page sees the same frames through the same detectors and the same zoom.py, so nothing here separates memory that indexes pictures from memory that indexes text about pictures. The case for the multimodal half is the design argument and the incident record — the 4 detector flags a text-only reader would have had to take on faith, the GUI layouts no log line describes — not a controlled number. It is the cheapest missing measurement on the page, and the one most worth having.

The open case is the dragon's tail. Same-task relay there moved the floor up and the ceiling down — both children of an 11/24 parent landed at 9/24. The tasks share only their first 8 milestones; the dragon's remaining 16 run out past the overworld into the End, and the parent memory holds almost nothing verified about that stretch. The child inherits a confident record of the prefix and silence exactly where it needs help, and appears to spend its budget consolidating the known part. Whether that is a defect of the memory schema or of what a 12,000-step episode can reach is the question the next wave has to separate.

What runs next

Five things, each aimed at the weakest joint above. wmlite is the arm that has not run: one compiled document over the same log, no graph, no ops, no discipline. Until it runs, “compiling beats grepping” and “the full apparatus beats grepping” are the same measurement. More seeds per cell — every number here is one run at one seed, and the diamond reversal in regime 1 rests on a single pair, which is exactly the kind of result that dissolves under replication. dm17 ← dm16 asks whether a chain keeps compounding after the task is solved, or whether a memory that closed the task has nothing left to add. kd17 ← dm16 is the strongest cross-task probe available: seed the dragon from the run that went all the way to the diamond, and see whether a fully-verified overworld prefix buys progress in the stretch where same-task inheritance regressed. A text-only memory arm — same compilation, same induction, frames still written to disk but never openable — is what turns the multimodal half of the design from an argument into a measurement.

Status — all three regimes have landed on both tasks at the 12,000-step budget, and every number above is current as of that wave.
